h1:
First Time in Sukhothai
What to Know + Itineraries
intro: Sukhothai is easier to get around than you'd think, but first-timers who show up with no plan usually trip over two things: the Old City and the New City are in completely different spots, almost 12 km apart, and the historical park is split into several zones, each charging its own entry fee. So we've pulled everything worth knowing before you set off into one place, then added a few itineraries to pick from depending on how much time you have — anywhere from half a day to three days.

blocks.html: First, the big picture. Sukhothai is a small province in Thailand's lower north, roughly 440 km from Bangkok. The star attraction is Sukhothai Historical Park — Thailand's first capital, over 700 years old, known worldwide as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The heart of the trip is cycling among the ancient ruins in the Old City, then working your way through as many bowls of Sukhothai noodles as you can manage.

blocks.text: Thing #1 — Old City vs New City: don't book in the wrong zone

blocks.html: This is what first-timers get wrong most often. Sukhothai has two towns that aren't next to each other. The Old City is the area around the historical park, in Mueang Kao district. The New City is the provincial town proper, with malls, markets, the bus station, and the hospital. The two are about 12 km apart — a 15–20 minute drive.

items: Want to wake up and cycle straight into the park — stay in the Old City. There are guesthouses and small resorts ringing the park, close enough to walk to the gate.

Arriving by tour bus, or want to be near restaurants and convenience stores — stay in the New City. There are more places to choose from across a wider price range, but you'll need to ride out to the park every morning.
Here for just one night — we'd stay in the Old City. You cut the commute and get more actual sightseeing time.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.html: A blue songthaew (shared pickup truck) runs a regular route between the two towns for around 30 THB a trip — but service stops in the early evening. If you plan to head back late, rent a motorbike or arrange a ride in advance.

blocks.text: Thing #2 — Park entry fees are charged by zone

blocks.html: Sukhothai Historical Park is divided into several zones, each with its own entry fee. If you plan to see it all, the combined ticket works out cheaper. The prices below are the Thai rate (latest available info — it can change, so double-check at the ticket booth).

items: Inner zone (central) — 20 THB for Thais. This is where you'll find Wat Mahathat, Wat Si Sawai, and Wat Traphang Ngoen, right in the middle of the park.
Northern zone — 20 THB for Thais. Home to Wat Si Chum (with its giant seated Buddha, Phra Achana) and Wat Phra Phai Luang.
Western zone — 20 THB for Thais. Wat Saphan Hin and Wat Chedi Ngam sit up on the hills here.
Combined ticket (all zones) — 40 THB for Thais / 400 THB for foreigners. Worth it if you're going to cycle every zone.
Free entry — students, monks, and visitors aged 60 and over (bring your ID).

blocks.title: Opening hours
blocks.html: The park is open daily 6:30 AM–7:30 PM, and stays open until 9:00 PM on Saturdays, when the ruins are beautifully lit at night. If you're here on a Saturday, don't miss sunset at Wat Mahathat.

blocks.text: Thing #3 — A rental bike is the star of the show

blocks.html: The Old City was practically made for cycling: flat, shady, with short hops between temples. Bike rental shops line the park entrance and most guesthouses, charging around 30 THB a day — rent for two days and you'll often get a rate of about 50 THB. Some shops have e-bikes and pedal-trishaw rides (around 200 THB an hour) for anyone who'd rather not cycle.

items.name: Standard bike
items.blurb: The popular pick at around 30 THB/day. Great for the flat inner zone — easy riding even if you're rusty.

items.name: E-bike / motorbike
items.blurb: Worth it if you're heading out to the northern and western zones farther afield. Saves your legs and your time.

items.name: Pedal-trishaw with driver
items.blurb: A local rider takes you around for about 200 THB/hour. Good for older travelers or families.

blocks.text: Thing #4 — The food you have to try

blocks.html: You can't come all this way and skip Sukhothai noodles — thin rice noodles, blanched, with yardlong beans, roasted peanuts, crispy pork rind, and red pork, in a broth that leans sweet-and-sour. It's a regional taste that's hard to find done right anywhere else. The other dish to try is khao poep: steamed rice-flour sheets, similar to a fresh noodle roll, wrapped around minced pork and vegetables and ladled with broth. Several of the famous spots have been open more than 40 years.

items: Sukhothai noodles — the standout shops are in both the Old City and the New City, many right along the road before the park gate. Around 40–60 THB a bowl.
Khao poep — a local dish considered the province's signature plate. The old-timer shops in the New City have been going for decades.
Old City walking street — open some evenings near the park, with local street food and that sunset-behind-the-ruins atmosphere.

blocks.text: Plan A — 1 day (in early, out by evening)

blocks.html: Good for anyone passing through on the way up north, or flying in early and out the same evening. Focus on the inner-zone highlights plus Wat Si Chum.

items.note: It helps the whole park make more sense

items.activity: Return the bike and head out

blocks.text: Plan B — 2 days, 1 night (the sweet spot)

blocks.html: This is the one we'd recommend most for first-timers. You get to see every zone of the park without rushing, plus sunset and the walking street. Staying in the Old City is the most convenient.

items.activity: Arrive in Sukhothai, check in to an Old City stay, rent a bike
items.note: Drop your bags and you can head straight out

items.activity: Enter the inner zone for Wat Mahathat, Wat Sa Si, Wat Si Sawai
items.note: Late afternoon, the sun softens — easy riding

items.activity: Wait for sunset at Wat Mahathat
items.note: Golden light hitting the chedi — the image people remember Sukhothai by

items.activity: Dinner around the Old City, walk the walking street (if it's on)
items.note: Try the local street food

blocks.title: Northern zone, western zone, and heading home

items.activity: Cycle into the park at first light, starting at Wat Si Chum
items.note: Very early means few people — great shots of Phra Achana

items.activity: See Wat Phra Phai Luang in the northern zone
items.note: An old group of ruins that not everyone makes it to

items.activity: Cross to the western zone, cycle up to Wat Saphan Hin to see Phra Attharot
items.note: A standing Buddha over 12 m tall on the hill, with a wide view over the Old City

items.activity: One last bowl of Sukhothai noodles or khao poep
items.note: Hit the shop you didn't get to yesterday

items.activity: Return the bike and head home
items.note: Leave time to pick up gold-thread textiles and Sangkhalok ceramics as souvenirs

blocks.html: If you have time to spare, spend day three out of town at Si Satchanalai, another historical park about 70 km to the north. It's quiet, set among the forest, and far less crowded than the Old City in Sukhothai.

items.activity: Follow Plan B (inner, northern, western zones) at an unhurried pace
items.note: You'll have time to add a café and a museum or two

items.activity: Drive or rent a car to Si Satchanalai Historical Park
items.note: About 70 km, roughly an hour

items.activity: Cycle around Wat Chang Lom and Wat Chedi Chet Thaeo in the forest
items.note: A different feel from Sukhothai — shadier, fewer people

items.activity: Try the noodles Si Satchanalai is known for
items.note: Mi phan, khao poep, and khao op are the local specialties here

items.activity: Stop by the Thuriang kilns and Sangkhalok ceramics for souvenirs
items.note: The ancient pottery that's distinctive to this area

items.activity: Head home

faq.q: First time in Sukhothai — should I stay in the Old City or the New City?
faq.a: If you're mainly here for the park and short on time, the Old City is the most convenient — you can wake up and cycle straight to the park gate. But if you're arriving by tour bus or want to be near restaurants and convenience stores, the New City has more options. The two are about 12 km apart, a 15–20 minute drive.

faq.q: How many days do I need for Sukhothai Historical Park?
faq.a: Half a day to a full day covers the inner-zone highlights and Wat Si Chum. But if you want to see every zone without rushing and catch sunset, go for 2 days and 1 night. Three days makes sense if you're also continuing on to Si Satchanalai.

faq.q: How much is entry to Sukhothai Historical Park?
faq.a: It's charged by zone — inner, northern, and western — at 20 THB each for Thais, or a combined all-zone ticket for 40 THB. For foreigners the combined ticket is 400 THB. Students, monks, and visitors aged 60 and over get in free.

faq.q: Do I need to rent a bike, or can I walk?
faq.a: You can walk, but it's tiring and slow — the temples are spread out. We'd rent a bike for around 30 THB a day; it's easy riding since the ground is flat and shady. If cycling isn't for you, there are e-bikes and pedal-trishaws for around 200 THB an hour.

faq.q: What food should I try in Sukhothai?
faq.a: Sukhothai noodles are number one — a sweet-and-sour bowl with yardlong beans, roasted peanuts, and crispy pork rind. Next is khao poep, the province's signature dish. Both are easy to find in the Old City and the New City alike.
